title: 06 · Valuing Tencent: a sum-of-the-parts DCF
text:
Setup: packages, shared functions, extracted financials, market inputs
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(tidyverse); library(knitr) })
source("../../R/valuation_dcf.R")
source("../../R/data_tencent.R")
source("../../R/plots.R")

data_dir <- "../../data/processed"
d <- read_tencent(file.path(data_dir, "tencent_financials.csv"))
mkt_in <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "tencent_market_inputs.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
m_in <- setNames(mkt_in$value, mkt_in$item)
betas <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "betas_module01.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
b_tc <- betas |> filter(symbol == "0700.HK")

tv <- function(item, fy, ...) tval(d, item, fy, ...)
chk <- check_tencent(d)
stopifnot(all(abs(as.matrix(chk$identities[, -1])) < 0.5, na.rm = TRUE), chk$n_disagree == 0)

price <- m_in[["price_0700_hk"]]; fx <- m_in[["fx_cny_hkd"]]
rf <- m_in[["rf_cgb_10y"]]; erp <- m_in[["erp_china"]]
yrs <- as.character(2021:2025)
Forecast anchors from the reports
segs <- c(`Value-added services` = "rev_vas", `Marketing services` = "rev_marketing",
          `FinTech & business services` = "rev_fintech_business")
rev2025 <- c(sapply(segs, tv, fy = "2025"), Others = tv("rev_others", "2025"))
h1 <- function(it, y) tv(paste0(it, "_h1"), y)
g_h1_total <- h1("revenue", "2026H1") / h1("revenue", "2025H1") - 1
g2026 <- c(sapply(segs, \(s) h1(s, "2026H1") / h1(s, "2025H1") - 1), Others = g_h1_total)

capex_total <- function(y) -(tv("capex_ppe_paid", y) + tv("intangibles_paid", y) + tv("land_use_rights_paid", y))
capex_hist <- c(capex_total("2021"), sapply(yrs, capex_total))          # FY2020 set equal to FY2021
rev_hist <- sapply(yrs, \(y) tv("revenue", y))
fcf_hist <- sapply(yrs, \(y) tv("cfo", y)) - sapply(yrs, capex_total) + sapply(yrs, \(y) tv("lease_principal_paid", y))
media_2025 <- -tv("intangibles_paid", "2025")
capex2026 <- 2 * h1("capex_reported", "2026H1") + media_2025
margin0 <- h1("ebitda", "2026H1") / h1("revenue", "2026H1")
tax_eff <- sapply(c("2024", "2025"), \(y) -tv("income_tax", y) / (tv("profit_before_tax", y) - tv("share_of_associates", y)))
lease_pct <- mean(sapply(yrs, \(y) -tv("lease_principal_paid", y)) / rev_hist)
capex_pre_ai <- mean((capex_hist[-1] / rev_hist)[c("2021", "2022", "2023")])

base <- list(rev2025 = rev2025, g2026 = g2026, capex_hist = capex_hist,
             capex2026 = capex2026, ebitda_margin0 = margin0)

# Balance sheet at the valuation date (30 June 2026) and share count
bs <- list(cash = tv("cash", "2026H1"), term_deposits = tv("term_deposits_others", "2026H1"),
           borrowings = -tv("borrowings_total", "2026H1"), notes = -tv("notes_total", "2026H1"),
           listed_bn = tv("listed_investments_fv_bn", "2026H1"),
           unlisted_bn = tv("unlisted_investments_bv_bn", "2026H1"), nci = tv("nci_equity", "2026H1"))
shares <- tv("shares_diluted_wavg_q2_m", "2026H1")
Cost of capital
beta_base <- b_tc$beta_blume                                # Module 01, Blume-adjusted
debt_val <- bs$borrowings + bs$notes
equity_val <- price * shares / fx                           # market cap in RMB million
gross_debt <- function(y) tv("borrowings_noncurrent", y) + tv("borrowings_current", y) +
  tv("notes_noncurrent", y) + tv("notes_current", y)
kd <- -tv("interest_paid", "2025") / mean(c(gross_debt("2024"), gross_debt("2025")))
tax_base <- round(mean(tax_eff), 2)
w <- wacc_calc(beta_base, rf, erp, kd, tax_base, equity_val, debt_val)
Base case DCF and bridge
p_base <- list(growth_mult = 1, g_terminal = 0.02, ebitda_margin_target = margin0,
               capex_intensity_ss = 0.10, tax = tax_base, lease_pct = lease_pct,
               wacc = w$wacc, n = 10, k_norm = 5)
hd_base <- 0.20                                             # holding discount on investments
run <- function(p, hd = hd_base) {
  r <- tencent_dcf(base, p)
  b <- sotp_bridge(r$pv$ev, bs, hd, fx, shares)
  list(dcf = r, bridge = b, value = b$per_share_hkd)
}
bc <- run(p_base)
val_at <- function(...) run(modifyList(p_base, list(...)))$value
upside <- bc$value / price - 1
Reverse DCF: what the price implies
implied <- function(f, lo, hi) tryCatch(uniroot(\(x) f(x) - price, c(lo, hi))$root, error = function(e) NA)
imp_wacc <- implied(\(x) val_at(wacc = x), 0.05, 0.30)
imp_ke <- (imp_wacc - w$w_d * w$kd_after_tax) / (1 - w$w_d)
imp_erp <- (imp_ke - rf) / beta_base
imp_capex <- implied(\(x) val_at(capex_intensity_ss = x), 0.05, 0.45)
imp_growth <- implied(\(x) val_at(growth_mult = x), -4, 1.5)
wacc_of <- function(e) wacc_calc(beta_base, rf, e, kd, tax_base, equity_val, debt_val)$wacc

grid <- expand_grid(erp = seq(0.04, 0.11, by = 0.0025), capex = seq(0.08, 0.30, by = 0.005)) |>
  mutate(value = map2_dbl(erp, capex, \(e, c) val_at(wacc = wacc_of(e), capex_intensity_ss = c)))
Monte Carlo: 10,000 draws over the uncertain inputs
set.seed(2026)
n_sim <- 10000
draws <- tibble(
  beta = rnorm(n_sim, beta_base, b_tc$se_beta),
  erp = runif(n_sim, 0.045, 0.080),
  g_terminal = runif(n_sim, 0.005, 0.025),
  growth_mult = runif(n_sim, 0.6, 1.3),
  margin = rnorm(n_sim, margin0, 0.025),
  capex_ss = runif(n_sim, 0.08, 0.20),
  tax = runif(n_sim, 0.17, 0.23),
  hd = runif(n_sim, 0.10, 0.40)
)
draws$wacc <- with(draws, map2_dbl(beta, erp, \(b, e) wacc_calc(b, rf, e, kd, tax_base, equity_val, debt_val)$wacc))
draws$value <- pmap_dbl(draws, function(beta, erp, g_terminal, growth_mult, margin, capex_ss, tax, hd, wacc) {
  run(modifyList(p_base, list(wacc = wacc, g_terminal = g_terminal, growth_mult = growth_mult,
                              ebitda_margin_target = margin, capex_intensity_ss = capex_ss, tax = tax)), hd)$value
})
q <- quantile(draws$value, c(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95))
p_above <- mean(draws$value > price)
# Which inputs move value most? Standardised regression of value on the draws.
drivers <- lm(scale(value) ~ scale(erp) + scale(beta) + scale(capex_ss) + scale(growth_mult) +
                scale(margin) + scale(g_terminal) + scale(tax) + scale(hd), data = draws)
drv <- tibble(term = names(coef(drivers))[-1], coef = coef(drivers)[-1]) |>
  mutate(term = gsub("scale\\(|\\)", "", term)) |> arrange(desc(abs(coef)))

title: 06 · Valuing Tencent: a sum-of-the-parts DCF
text:
Question
Tencent (0700.HK) is one of Asia’s largest companies by market value: WeChat, one of the world’s largest video-game businesses, a payments network, cloud services and a large portfolio of stakes in other companies. Is its market value justified by the cash its businesses will generate? And if not, what is the price assuming?
One company, one share, three quotes. Tencent’s ordinary shares trade in Hong Kong in HKD (0700.HK) and on HKEX’s renminbi counter (80700.HK). American Depositary Receipts trade over the counter in the US (TCEHY, one ADR per share). Mainland investors buy 0700 through Stock Connect. These are all claims on the same pool of shares, so the valuation uses the total diluted share count and one price: HK$386.6. The RMB counter (CNY 329.2) and the ADR (US$49.74) trade at the same value after currency conversion. Adding the listings together would count the same shares two or three times.

title: 06 · Valuing Tencent: a sum-of-the-parts DCF
text:
Data
The financials come from Tencent’s annual reports for 2022–2025 and its 2026 interim report, downloaded from Tencent’s investor-relations site. A script (scripts/extract_tencent.py) extracts each figure with its report and page number. Two checks run every time this page is built:

Accounting identities: segments sum to revenue, revenue less cost of revenue equals gross profit, profit before tax less tax equals profit, and cash plus deposits less debt equals Tencent’s reported net cash. All hold to the RMB million in every year.
Cross-report agreement: each report also shows the prior year, so 174 figures are extracted twice from different reports. All agree, except where Tencent has restated: in 2023 it moved investment gains below the operating-profit line, and it later redefined non-IFRS operating profit. The latest (restated) figures are used throughout.



Show code
hist <- tibble(
  Item = c("Revenue", "  Value-added services", "  Marketing services", "  FinTech & business services",
           "Operating profit (IFRS, restated)", "EBITDA margin", "Capital expenditure (cash)",
           "Free cash flow", "Share-based compensation", "Diluted shares (billion)"),
  !!!set_names(map(yrs, function(y) c(
    tv("revenue", y), tv("rev_vas", y), tv("rev_marketing", y), tv("rev_fintech_business", y),
    if (y == "2021") tv("operating_profit", y, restated = TRUE) else tv("operating_profit", y),
    NA, capex_total(y), fcf_hist[[y]], tv("sbc_equity", y), tv("shares_diluted_wavg_m", y))), yrs))
for (y in yrs) hist[[y]] <- ifelse(hist$Item == "EBITDA margin",
                                   sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (tv("operating_profit", y, restated = y == "2021") -
                                                              tv("other_gains", y) * (y != "2021") +
                                                              tv("dep_ppe", y) + tv("dep_rou", y) + tv("amort_intangibles", y)) / tv("revenue", y)),
                                   formatC(hist[[y]] / 1000, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ","))
hist$`2021`[hist$Item == "EBITDA margin"] <- "–"

Three features of the history drive the valuation. Growth has resumed: revenue rose 23% over 2023–25, and first-half 2026 revenue was up 10.1% year on year, led by marketing services (20.9%). Margins have widened: the EBITDA margin reached 42.4% in the first half of 2026. Capital spending has exploded: cash capex rose from 47 billion in 2023 to 113 billion in 2025, and Tencent spent RMB 84.7 billion in the first half of 2026 alone, mostly on AI infrastructure.

title: 06 · Valuing Tencent: a sum-of-the-parts DCF
text:
Model
Operating forecast (FY2026–FY2035). Each segment’s revenue grows in FY2026 at its first-half 2026 year-on-year rate. From FY2027, that rate fades linearly to the terminal growth rate by FY2035. The EBITDA margin starts at its first-half 2026 level (42.4%). Margin, rather than operating profit, is the driver, so that the depreciation from today’s capex wave is charged against profit as it arrives. EBITDA here is after share-based compensation, which is treated as a real cost.
Capital spending and depreciation. FY2026 capex is set to twice the first-half figure plus media-content spending at its 2025 level (RMB 195 billion, 24% of revenue). It then fades to a steady-state share of revenue by FY2030 (base case 10%, close to the pre-AI average of 9.4%). Depreciation is five-year straight-line on actual and forecast capex. Free cash flow is \(\text{EBITDA} - \text{tax on EBIT} - \text{capex} - \text{lease payments}\), with tax at 20% (Tencent’s effective rate on operating profit in 2024–25: 20.8% and 18.7%).
Discounting. The valuation date is 30 June 2026, the latest balance sheet. Only the second half of FY2026 is counted, then mid-year flows, and a Gordon terminal value from FY2035 at 2% growth.


Show code

Sum of the parts. Tencent’s stakes in other companies are valued separately, not through the cash-flow forecast. Their profits are excluded from the operating forecast to avoid counting them twice. Both carry a 20% holding discount, reflecting tax on disposal, illiquidity and the market’s usual conglomerate discount. Cash and term deposits are added, debt and minority interests subtracted.

title: 06 · Valuing Tencent: a sum-of-the-parts DCF
text:
Results

Base case


Show code
per_share <- bc$bridge$parts / shares * fx
br <- tibble(part = c("Operating business", "Cash & deposits", "Debt", "Listed stakes (net)",
                      "Unlisted stakes (net)", "Minority interests"),
             value = unname(per_share)) |>
  mutate(end = cumsum(value), start = lag(end, default = 0), part = factor(part, levels = part))
br <- bind_rows(br, tibble(part = factor("Value per share"), value = sum(per_share), start = 0, end = sum(per_share))) |>
  mutate(part = factor(part, levels = c(levels(br$part), "Value per share")),
         kind = case_when(part == "Value per share" ~ "total", value >= 0 ~ "add", TRUE ~ "subtract"))
ggplot(br, aes(x = part)) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = as.numeric(part) - 0.38, xmax = as.numeric(part) + 0.38,
                ymin = pmin(start, end), ymax = pmax(start, end), fill = kind)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = price, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#52514e") +
  annotate("label", x = 4, y = price, label = sprintf("Share price HK$%.1f", price),
           size = 3.2, colour = "#52514e", label.size = 0, fill = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(y = pmax(start, end), label = if_else(kind == "total", sprintf("%.0f", value), sprintf("%+.0f", value))),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3.1, colour = "#0b0b0b") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) str_wrap(x, 12)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(add = "#2a78d6", subtract = "#e34948", total = "#0b0b0b"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0("HK$", x)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_report() + theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8.5))








Figure 1: From operating value to value per share (HK$ per share, base case).





The base case values Tencent at HK$827 per share, 114% above the price. The operating business is worth HK$741 per share, of which 69% comes from the terminal value (typical for a long-lived business). The forecast reaches RMB 1431 billion of revenue and RMB 354 billion of free cash flow in FY2035. That free cash flow is 25% of revenue, in line with the 24% Tencent achieved in 2025.

What the price implies

  geom_raster(aes(fill = value), interpolate = TRUE) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = value), breaks = price, colour = "#0b0b0b", linewidth = 0.9) +

  annotate("point", x = p_base$capex_intensity_ss, y = erp, size = 3, shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = "#0b0b0b") +
  annotate("label", x = p_base$capex_intensity_ss + 0.006, y = erp, label = sprintf("Base case: HK$%.0f", bc$value),

  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Tencent's price implies a large risk premium, permanent AI spending, or both",
       subtitle = "DCF value per share by equity risk premium and steady-state capex (% of revenue)",
       x = "Steady-state capital expenditure (% of revenue)", y = "Equity risk premium",
       caption = sprintf("Other inputs at base case. Risk-free %s (China 10y), beta %s. Blue = above price, red = below.",
                         pct(rf, 2), num(beta_base))) +
  theme_report() + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.justification = "center")
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave("figures/key_chart.png", p_imp, width = 8.5, height = 5.2, dpi = 200, bg = "white")
p_imp








Figure 2: Value per share across the two assumptions that matter most: the equity risk premium and steady-state capital spending. The black line is today’s share price; combinations on it justify the price exactly. The point marks the base case.





Holding everything else at the base case, the price is justified by any one of the following:

a WACC of 13.6%, which is a cost of equity of about 15% and an equity risk premium of 12%, more than twice Damodaran’s 5.14% for China;
steady-state capex of 28% of revenue, permanently, against 9% before the AI build-out and about 24% at the 2026 peak;
revenue growth that reverses: the FY2026 growth rates would have to be multiplied by -1.30 from FY2027 onward, meaning several years of shrinking revenue.

Each of these alone is extreme. In combination they are not. The contour shows, for example, that a 10% equity risk premium with capex at 15% of revenue, or 8% with 20%, both land close to the price. A gap of 3–5 points over the rating-based risk premium is what a specific “China discount” on offshore-listed Chinese companies would look like. Plausible sources are regulatory risk (as in the 2021 platform crackdown), the VIE ownership structure (foreign shareholders own contractual claims, not the Chinese operating companies themselves), and US–China tensions. This analysis measures the size of the gap but does not test its causes.


Monte Carlo


Show code

  geom_histogram(bins = 80, fill = "#2a78d6", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = price, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#0b0b0b") +
  annotate("text", x = price, y = Inf, label = sprintf("Price HK$%.0f", price), hjust = 1.05, vjust = 1.5, size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = q["50%"], y = Inf, label = sprintf("Median HK$%.0f", q["50%"]), hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1.5, size = 3.2,
           colour = "#2a78d6") +

         g_terminal = "Terminal growth", tax = "Tax rate", hd = "Holding discount on investments")

         capex_ss = "Uniform 8%–20%", growth_mult = "Uniform 0.6–1.3", margin = sprintf("Normal(%s, 2.5 pts)", pct(margin0)),
         g_terminal = "Uniform 0.5%–2.5%", tax = "Uniform 17%–23%", hd = "Uniform 10%–40%")

The ranges are deliberately wide, and the equity risk premium range extends well above the rating-based figure. Even so, 96% of draws value Tencent above its price, and the 5th percentile is HK$391. The two inputs that matter most are the equity risk premium and steady-state capex, the same two that the reverse DCF singles out. Margins, growth and terminal growth matter less, with roughly half the influence. The valuation question is about how much risk to charge and how much cash AI will consume, not about whether Tencent’s businesses keep growing.

title: 06 · Valuing Tencent: a sum-of-the-parts DCF
text:
Limitations

The cost of capital is the crux, and it is contested. A risk-free rate of 1.61% reflects China’s low-inflation, low-rate economy, and a rating-based risk premium may not capture the risks offshore investors actually price. Readers who believe the market’s implied premium is correct will conclude the price is fair. This analysis makes the size of that premium explicit, but it cannot settle it.
AI capex is unprecedented. No history exists for how long the current spending lasts or what it earns. The model assumes it normalises by FY2030; the reverse DCF shows how much depends on that.
No consensus forecasts. The forecast is built from Tencent’s reported trends, not analyst estimates, which would usually be a cross-check.
Investments are marked at one date. The listed portfolio’s fair value fell by RMB 186 billion in the first half of 2026 alone. Every RMB 100 billion is worth about HK$10 per share.
Simplifications. Minority interests are at book value. Working-capital changes are set to zero (Tencent’s deferred revenue makes working capital a small source of cash). Lease payments are treated as an operating cost rather than debt. The valuation is as at 30 June 2026 and is compared with a November 2026 price without rolling forward. Rolling forward to the price date would raise it by about 2.5%.
Not investment advice. This is an analytical exercise in valuation methods using public information.

text:
Setup: packages, shared functions, USD excess returns
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(tidyverse); library(knitr); library(glmnet) })
source("../../R/models_linear.R")
source("../../R/models_factor.R")
source("../../R/data_factors.R")
source("../../R/plots.R")

data_dir <- "../../data/processed"
universe <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "universe.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
ret <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "returns_monthly.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
fx  <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "fx_monthly.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
mkt <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "market_monthly.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
ff  <- get_french_apac("../../data/raw/french")

# Same test assets as Module 03: USD excess returns over the US T-bill
panel <- ret |>
  inner_join(universe, by = c("symbol" = "ticker")) |>
  inner_join(fx, by = c("market", "month")) |>
  inner_join(ff, by = "month") |>
  mutate(ex = (1 + ret) * (1 + fx) - 1 - RF)
wide <- panel |> select(month, symbol, ex) |> pivot_wider(names_from = symbol, values_from = ex) |> arrange(month)
Y <- as.matrix(select(wide, -month)); months <- wide$month
Fac <- ff |> filter(month %in% months) |> arrange(month)
T_ <- nrow(Y); N_ <- ncol(Y)
stock_market <- universe$market[match(colnames(Y), universe$ticker)]
stock_sector <- universe$sector[match(colnames(Y), universe$ticker)]
short <- function(s) sub("\\.(AX|HK|SI)$", "", s)
Principal components and the two noise benchmarks
pc <- pca_returns(Y)                                  # correlation-matrix PCA
mp <- mp_upper(N_, T_)                                # Marchenko–Pastur edge
pa <- parallel_analysis(Y, reps = 500, prob = 0.95)   # permutation benchmark
n_mp <- sum(pc$values > mp); n_pa <- sum(pc$values > pa)
k_sig <- min(n_mp, n_pa)
stopifnot(n_mp == n_pa)                               # text reports one agreed number
Linking components to observable factors: correlations, canonical correlation, LASSO
ff_names <- c("MKT", "SMB", "HML", "RMW", "CMA", "WML")
X_ff <- as.matrix(Fac[, ff_names])

# Candidate observables beyond Fama–French: each local index (USD excess) and currencies
loc <- mkt |> inner_join(fx, by = c("market", "month")) |> filter(month %in% months) |>
  mutate(usd = (1 + mkt) * (1 + fx) - 1) |> select(market, month, usd) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = market, values_from = usd) |> arrange(month)
fxw <- fx |> filter(month %in% months) |> pivot_wider(names_from = market, values_from = fx) |> arrange(month)
X_all <- cbind(X_ff, `ASX index` = loc$ASX - Fac$RF, `HK index` = loc$HKEX - Fac$RF,
               `SG index` = loc$SGX - Fac$RF, AUD = fxw$ASX, SGD = fxw$SGX)

cors <- cor(pc$scores[, 1:4], X_all)
nm_of <- function(s) paste0(universe$name[match(s, universe$ticker)])
o1 <- order(pc$vectors[, 1])
top_pc1 <- paste(nm_of(rownames(pc$vectors)[rev(o1)[1:4]]), collapse = ", ")
bot_pc1 <- paste(nm_of(rownames(pc$vectors)[o1[1:4]]), collapse = ", ")
cc <- cancor(pc$scores[, 1:k_sig], X_ff)$cor

set.seed(1)
lasso <- map_dfr(1:4, function(k) {
  cv <- cv.glmnet(scale(X_all), pc$scores[, k], alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
  b <- coef(cv, s = "lambda.1se")[-1, 1]
  fit <- predict(cv, scale(X_all), s = "lambda.1se")
  tibble(PC = paste0("PC", k),
         `Selected (standardised coefficient)` = if (any(b != 0))
           paste(sprintf("%s %+.2f", names(b)[b != 0], b[b != 0])[order(-abs(b[b != 0]))], collapse = ", ") else "none",
         R2 = 1 - sum((pc$scores[, k] - fit)^2) / sum((pc$scores[, k] - mean(pc$scores[, k]))^2))
})
Out-of-sample pricing: factors from half the stocks (2011–18), tested on the other half (2019–25)
early <- months < as.Date("2019-01-01")
fac_models <- list(CAPM = "MKT", `Fama–French 3` = c("MKT", "SMB3", "HML"),
                   `Fama–French 5` = c("MKT", "SMB", "HML", "RMW", "CMA"))
n_splits <- 200
set.seed(42)
oos <- map_dfr(seq_len(n_splits), function(s) {
  # stratified random half of the stocks builds the factors; the rest are test assets
  A <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_len(N_), stock_market), \(ix) sample(ix, floor(length(ix) / 2))))
  B <- setdiff(seq_len(N_), A)
  pA <- pca_returns(Y[early, A])
  pcs <- map_dfr(1:5, function(k) {
    Fk <- Y[!early, A] %*% eigenportfolio_weights(pA, k)
    g <- grs_test(Y[!early, B], Fk)
    tibble(model = paste0("PCA, ", k, if (k == 1) " factor" else " factors"),
           rms = 12 * sqrt(mean(g$alpha^2)), p = g$p)
  })
  obs <- imap_dfr(fac_models, function(f, nm) {
    g <- grs_test(Y[!early, B], as.matrix(Fac[!early, f]))
    tibble(model = nm, rms = 12 * sqrt(mean(g$alpha^2)), p = g$p)
  })
  bind_rows(pcs, obs) |> mutate(split = s)
})
oos_sum <- oos |> group_by(model) |>
  summarise(rms_med = median(rms), rms_lo = quantile(rms, 0.1), rms_hi = quantile(rms, 0.9),
            reject = mean(p < 0.05), .groups = "drop")
best_pca <- oos_sum |> filter(str_starts(model, "PCA")) |> slice_min(rms_med, n = 1)

  select(split, model, rms) |> pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = rms) |>
  summarise(m = mean(.data[[best_pca$model]] < CAPM)) |> pull(m)

title: 04 · Statistical factors: how many risks drive APAC returns?
text:
Question
Modules 01 and 03 started from factors chosen in advance: the market, then the Fama–French characteristics. Arbitrage Pricing Theory (Ross, 1976) only says that some small set of common factors drives returns and earns premia. It doesn’t say which ones. This module lets the data choose. How many common factors are in the returns of APAC large caps, what are they, and do they line up with the factors used in Module 03?

title: 04 · Statistical factors: how many risks drive APAC returns?
text:
Method
Principal components. Each stock’s monthly USD excess return (same data as Module 03, Feb 2011–Dec 2025, 179 months) is standardised. The 51 × 51 correlation matrix is decomposed as \(\mathbf R = \mathbf V \boldsymbol\Lambda \mathbf V'\). Each eigenvalue \(\lambda_j\) is the variance captured by component j, and each column of \(\mathbf V\) gives the stocks’ loadings on it. Using correlations rather than covariances stops the most volatile stocks from dominating.
How many factors? Some eigenvalues will look large even in pure noise, so each is compared with two benchmarks:

the Marchenko–Pastur upper edge, \(\lambda_+ = (1+\sqrt{N/T})^2 = 2.35\), the largest eigenvalue expected from \(N\) uncorrelated series of length \(T\);
parallel analysis: the 95th percentile of each eigenvalue across 500 data sets in which each stock’s returns are shuffled in time independently. Shuffling destroys the cross-correlation but keeps each stock’s fat-tailed distribution.

What are they? Components are compared with the six Fama–French factors and with five other observables (each local index and two currencies) using correlations, canonical correlation, and LASSO regressions (glmnet, penalty chosen by 10-fold cross-validation, one-standard-error rule).
Do they price? Components estimated on the same data they are tested on would price that data almost by construction. So the test is out of sample in two dimensions. Each of 200 random splits divides the stocks in half, stratified by market. Eigenportfolios (traded versions of the components) are built from one half using 2011–18 data, and the GRS test is run on the other half in 2019–25. The CAPM and Fama–French models are tested on the same stocks and months.

Results

Three factors stand out from the noise

p_scree








Figure 1: Eigenvalues of the 51-stock correlation matrix (points), with the Marchenko–Pastur edge (dashed) and the 95th percentile from permuted data (line). Eigenvalues above both are treated as genuine common factors. The first eigenvalue is off the scale and labelled.





The first eigenvalue (22.0) is nearly ten times the noise edge. The second and third (4.36, 2.42) clear both benchmarks. From the fourth on (1.92, 1.63, …), the eigenvalues sit below both lines and are indistinguishable from what independent noise would produce. Together the three genuine factors explain 56% of the total variation, so most of each stock’s monthly movement remains stock-specific.


What the factors are

Out of sample, the statistical factors leave smaller pricing errors than the observable ones. The best, PCA, 3 factors, has a median RMS alpha of 8.2% a year and beats the CAPM in 92% of splits. The Fama–French models do no better than the CAPM here, consistent with Module 03. Most of the gain comes from the first component, though: a single statistical factor already does about as well as three to five. The intervals overlap substantially, and with only 84 test months GRS rarely rejects any model (power is low, so “not rejected” here is weak evidence of a good fit). Pricing errors are also larger here than in Module 03’s full-sample tests, partly because alphas estimated over seven years are noisier than over fifteen.

title: 04 · Statistical factors: how many risks drive APAC returns?
text:
Limitations

Survivor sample. As in Module 03, today’s large caps are the test assets, which biases alphas upward for every model. It does not affect the factor-count results, which concern covariances.
Stationarity. PCA assumes one stable covariance structure over 15 years. Module 01 found that betas shifted after 2020 (for example, the Chinese banks decoupled), so the loadings on PC2 in particular are averages over two regimes.
Labelling is interpretation. Components are defined only up to rotation within the significant set. The names given here describe the loadings but are not unique.
Small test. 51 stocks and a 7-year test window limit power. A broader universe (all regional stocks) would sharpen both the factor count and the pricing comparison.

title: 01 · CAPM and the market model across ASX, HKEX and SGX
text:
Setup: packages, shared functions, settings
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(tidyverse); library(knitr)
})
source("../../R/models_linear.R")
source("../../R/plots.R")

data_dir <- "../../data/processed"
nw_lag <- 4                                   # floor(4 (T/100)^(2/9)) for T = 188
break_month <- as.Date("2020-01-01")          # split for the stability test
roll_win <- 60                                # rolling-beta window (months)

universe <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "universe.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
ret <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "returns_monthly.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
mkt <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "market_monthly.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
rf  <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "rf_monthly.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# Panel of excess returns: stock and market both in excess of the local rate
panel <- ret |>
  inner_join(universe, by = c("symbol" = "ticker")) |>
  inner_join(mkt, by = c("market", "month")) |>
  inner_join(rf, by = c("market", "month")) |>
  mutate(ex = ret - rf, mex = mkt - rf,
         market = factor(market, levels = names(market_cols)))

n_months <- n_distinct(panel$month)
first_m <- format(min(panel$month), "%b %Y"); last_m <- format(max(panel$month), "%b %Y")
n_stock <- table(universe$market)
Market model for every stock, estimated in matrix form per market
# For each market: Y (T x N) = X B + E, X = [1, market excess return].
# One normal-equations solve gives all N alphas and betas; HAC errors per stock.
fit_market <- function(d) {
  wide <- d |> select(month, symbol, ex) |> pivot_wider(names_from = symbol, values_from = ex) |>
    arrange(month)
  f <- d |> distinct(month, mex) |> arrange(month)
  stopifnot(identical(wide$month, f$month))
  Y <- as.matrix(select(wide, -month)); X <- cbind(const = 1, mex = f$mex)
  map_dfr(colnames(Y), function(s) {
    fit <- ols_matrix(Y[, s], X)
    V <- hac_vcov(fit, nw_lag)
    ct <- coef_table(fit, V)
    tibble(symbol = s, alpha = ct$estimate[1], se_alpha = ct$se[1], p_alpha = ct$p[1],
           beta = ct$estimate[2], se_beta = ct$se[2],
           r2 = 1 - sum(fit$resid^2) / sum((Y[, s] - mean(Y[, s]))^2),
           idio_vol = sqrt(12 * fit$sigma2), total_vol = sqrt(12) * sd(Y[, s]))
  })
}

est <- panel |> group_by(market) |> group_modify(~ fit_market(.x)) |> ungroup() |>
  left_join(universe |> select(ticker, name, sector), by = c("symbol" = "ticker")) |>
  mutate(ticker = sub("\\.(AX|HK|SI)$", "", symbol),
         beta_lo = beta - 1.96 * se_beta, beta_hi = beta + 1.96 * se_beta,
         beta_blume = 2/3 * beta + 1/3,                # Blume (1971) adjustment toward 1
         p_alpha_bh = p.adjust(p_alpha, "BH"))         # false-discovery-rate correction

# Cross-check: the matrix estimator reproduces lm() for one stock
chk <- panel |> filter(symbol == "0700.HK")
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(coef(lm(ex ~ mex, chk))[2]),
                           est$beta[est$symbol == "0700.HK"], tolerance = 1e-10)))

mkt_summary <- est |> group_by(market) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_beta = median(beta), min_beta = min(beta), max_beta = max(beta),
            median_r2 = median(r2), share_beta_lt1 = mean(beta < 1), .groups = "drop")
n_alpha_raw <- sum(est$p_alpha < 0.05); n_alpha_bh <- sum(est$p_alpha_bh < 0.05)
Beta stability: split-sample test with HAC errors (general linear hypothesis)
# ex = a + b * mex + d0 * post + d1 * (mex x post) + e;  H0: d1 = 0 (beta unchanged)
stab <- panel |> group_by(market, symbol) |> group_modify(function(d, key) {
  post <- as.numeric(d$month >= break_month)
  X <- cbind(const = 1, mex = d$mex, post = post, mex_post = d$mex * post)
  fit <- ols_matrix(d$ex, X)
  V <- hac_vcov(fit, nw_lag)
  lh <- linear_hypothesis(fit, rbind(c(0, 0, 0, 1)), V = V)
  tibble(beta_pre = fit$coef["mex"], beta_post = fit$coef["mex"] + fit$coef["mex_post"],
         d_beta = fit$coef["mex_post"], p_change = lh["p"])
}) |> ungroup() |>
  mutate(p_change_bh = p.adjust(p_change, "BH"),
         ticker = sub("\\.(AX|HK|SI)$", "", symbol))

n_shift_bh <- sum(stab$p_change_bh < 0.05)
shift_up <- stab |> filter(p_change_bh < 0.05, d_beta > 0) |> arrange(desc(d_beta))
shift_dn <- stab |> filter(p_change_bh < 0.05, d_beta < 0) |> arrange(d_beta)
med_abs_shift <- median(abs(stab$d_beta))
rank_cor <- cor(stab$beta_pre, stab$beta_post, method = "spearman")

# Sector groups referred to in the text
stab <- stab |> left_join(universe |> select(ticker, sector), by = c("symbol" = "ticker"))
cn_banks <- stab |> filter(symbol %in% c("0939.HK", "1398.HK", "3988.HK"))
cn_banks_pre <- mean(cn_banks$beta_pre); cn_banks_post <- mean(cn_banks$beta_post)
cn_full <- mean(est$beta[est$symbol %in% cn_banks$symbol])
res <- stab |> filter(sector %in% c("Materials", "Energy"), symbol != "AMC.AX")  # Amcor is packaging
n_res <- nrow(res); n_res_down <- sum(res$d_beta < 0)
au_banks <- stab |> filter(market == "ASX", sector == "Banks")
stopifnot(n_res_down == n_res, all(au_banks$d_beta > 0), nrow(au_banks) == 4)  # text claims "all"

# Rolling 60-month betas
roll <- panel |> group_by(symbol) |> arrange(month) |> group_modify(function(d, key) {
  if (nrow(d) < roll_win) return(tibble())
  map_dfr(roll_win:nrow(d), function(k) {
    w <- d[(k - roll_win + 1):k, ]
    tibble(month = d$month[k], beta = cov(w$ex, w$mex) / var(w$mex))
  })
}) |> ungroup() |> left_join(universe, by = c("symbol" = "ticker"))
roll_range <- roll |> group_by(symbol) |> summarise(range = max(beta) - min(beta))

title: 01 · CAPM and the market model across ASX, HKEX and SGX
text:
Question
The CAPM prices a stock’s expected excess return off a single number, its beta against the market:
\[
r_{i,t} - r_{f,t} \;=\; \alpha_i + \beta_i\,(r_{m,t} - r_{f,t}) + \varepsilon_{i,t}.
\]
This module estimates that market model for large caps on the three main APAC exchanges. It asks three questions: how large and how precise the betas are, how much of each stock’s risk the market explains, and whether the betas stay put. Whether beta is actually priced in the cross-section of returns is tested in Module 03.

title: 01 · CAPM and the market model across ASX, HKEX and SGX
text:
Method
For each market, the excess returns of its N stocks are stacked into a T × N matrix and estimated in one step,
\[
\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{E}, \qquad \mathbf{X} = [\,\mathbf{1},\; \mathbf{r}_m - \mathbf{r}_f\,], \qquad \hat{\mathbf{B}} = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{Y}.
\]

Standard errors are Newey–West (Bartlett kernel, 4 lags), \(\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta) = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{S}}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\), allowing for heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation. The estimators are hand-written in R/models_linear.R and unit-tested against lm() and sandwich::NeweyWest to 10 decimal places (tests/).
Multiple testing: with 51 stocks, about 3 would show “significant” alphas or beta shifts at 5% by chance alone. p-values are therefore also reported after a Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction.
Stability is tested with a dummy-interaction model, \(r_i - r_f = a + b\,x + d_0\,\text{post} + d_1\,(x \times \text{post}) + \varepsilon\), where \(x\) is the market excess return and post = 1 from January 2020. The test is the general linear hypothesis \(H_0\!: d_1 = 0\) with HAC covariance. Rolling 60-month betas show the path between the two halves.

The shifts cluster by sector, which suggests real economic change rather than noise:

Chinese state banks (CCB, ICBC, Bank of China) went from moving more than the Hang Seng to moving about half as much. A plausible reading: after 2020 the index was driven by the Chinese tech and property sell-offs, while the state banks traded as policy-supported, high-dividend stocks.

Australian banks all became more market-sensitive. Rate-cycle news after COVID moved the whole ASX, and the banks are among its most rate-sensitive large caps.

The ranking of stocks by beta is only moderately persistent (Spearman correlation 0.49 between the two halves). In a perpetuity valuation with 3% growth and a 9% discount rate, that lowers the value by almost a quarter (from 1/0.06 to 1/0.078 times the cash flow).

title: 01 · CAPM and the market model across ASX, HKEX and SGX
text:
Limitations

Survivorship. These are today’s large caps, chosen with hindsight. Firms that shrank, were taken over or delisted (Hang Seng Bank is one) are missing, which biases average returns, and so alphas, upward. Betas are less affected.
Market proxies. Each index ETF tracks a cap-weighted index, which is the textbook choice. But the Hang Seng is concentrated in financials and Chinese tech, so Hong Kong betas are relative to that particular mix. ETF fees (about 0.05–0.10% a year) slightly lower the measured market return.
Local currency. Each market is analysed in its own currency against its own risk-free rate, which is right for a local investor. An AUD-based investor holding HK or SG stocks also bears currency risk, which is not modelled here.
Yahoo data. Adjusted closes can be wrong around corporate actions (Thai Beverage was excluded for this). The remaining data passed a screen for implausible moves, but this is not a vendor-grade database.

title: APAC Asset Pricing
text:
Do the asset-pricing models built on US data work in Asia-Pacific markets, and what do they imply for real valuation questions? Each module answers one question, opens with the answer, and feeds the next. The betas from Module 01 feed the cost of capital in Module 06, and the factor tests in Module 03 set up the cross-market comparison in Module 05.
Every model is written in matrix form (\(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\mathbf y\), GLS where errors are correlated, general linear hypotheses \(\mathbf C\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf 0\)). The hand-written estimators are unit-tested against lm(), sandwich and car, and against simulated data with known answers.

  inner_join(fx, by = c("market", "month")) |>

models <- list(
  "CAPM"          = c("MKT"),
  "Fama–French 3" = c("MKT", "SMB3", "HML"),

  F <- as.matrix(Fac[, f])
  g <- grs_test(Y, F)
  fit <- ols_matrix(Y, cbind(1, F))
  r2 <- 1 - colSums(fit$resid^2) / colSums(sweep(Y, 2, colMeans(Y))^2)
  # per-stock HAC t-stats on alpha
  p_alpha <- map_dbl(seq_len(N_), function(j) {
    fj <- ols_matrix(Y[, j], cbind(1, F)); coef_table(fj, hac_vcov(fj, 4))$p[1]
  })

       predicted = drop(t(fit$coef[-1, , drop = FALSE]) %*% colMeans(F)),  # beta' * mean factor
       realised = colMeans(Y))
})

  Model = nm, Factors = length(models[[nm]]),

  `RMS α (p.a.)` = 12 * sqrt(mean(r$alpha^2)),

  `Mean R²` = mean(r$r2),
  `Sharpe: factors` = sqrt(12) * r$grs$sharpe_factors,
  `Sharpe: tangency` = sqrt(12) * r$grs$sharpe_tangency))

  F <- as.matrix(Fac[, f]); colnames(F) <- f
  fm <- fama_macbeth(Y, F, intercept = TRUE)
  fm$factor_mean <- c(NA, colMeans(F))
  fm$model <- nm

})

A model “prices” the assets if, after controlling for the assets’ factor exposures, nothing is left over. Two tests check this. Time-series: are all the intercepts (alphas) jointly zero? Data

Test assets: the 51 large caps from Module 01 (ASX, HKEX, SGX), with monthly total returns converted to US dollars at month-end exchange rates. The sample runs from Feb 2011 to Dec 2025 (179 months).
Factors: Fama–French Asia Pacific ex Japan factors (Australia, Hong Kong, Singapore and New Zealand), in USD, with the US one-month T-bill as the risk-free rate, from the Kenneth French Data Library. They are built from all listed stocks in the region, not just our sample.
Why USD: the factors are USD returns on a regional portfolio, so the test assets have to be in the same currency and in excess of the same risk-free rate. Module 01 used local currency against local rates, which suits single-market betas.
Data access note: the French library was unreachable from the network used for this analysis, so the factor files are copies of the original files from the Internet Archive (dated February 2026, data to December 2025). French rebuilds the full history each month, so later versions can differ slightly. Provenance is recorded in the repository.

title: 03 · Testing pricing models: CAPM vs zero-beta CAPM vs Fama–French
text:
Method
All estimators are matrix-form functions in R/models_linear.R, each unit-tested against reference implementations and simulations.
Time series. For each model with K factors, \(\mathbf Y = \mathbf 1\boldsymbol\alpha' + \mathbf F\mathbf B' + \mathbf E\) is fitted to all 51 stocks at once. The Gibbons–Ross–Shanken statistic tests \(H_0: \boldsymbol\alpha = \mathbf 0\) jointly:
\[
\text{GRS} = \frac{T}{N}\,\frac{T-N-K}{T-K-1}\;\frac{\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}'\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}}{1 + \bar{\mathbf f}'\hat{\boldsymbol\Omega}^{-1}\bar{\mathbf f}} \;\sim\; F_{N,\;T-N-K}.
\]
It has a useful reading in terms of Sharpe ratios. GRS is large when the best portfolio of the test assets and the factors (the tangency portfolio) has a much higher Sharpe ratio than the factors alone.
Cross section. Fama–MacBeth two-pass regressions. Pass 1 estimates each stock’s betas over the full sample. Pass 2 regresses each month’s excess returns on those betas, \(r_{i,t} = \gamma_{0,t} + \boldsymbol\beta_i'\boldsymbol\gamma_t + \eta_{i,t}\), and averages the slopes. Standard errors use the Shanken (1992) correction for the fact that the betas are estimated. If a model holds, \(\gamma_0 = 0\) and each premium equals its factor’s mean return. A positive \(\gamma_0\) with a beta premium below the market premium is the zero-beta (Black, 1972) CAPM. A GLS version of the cross-sectional regression, weighting by the inverse residual covariance, is reported for the CAPM as a check.

Figure 1: Realised vs model-predicted average excess return for each stock (predicted = betas × average factor returns). Points on the dashed 45° line are priced perfectly; the vertical distance is the stock’s alpha.





The GRS statistics reject every model. Figure 1 shows the shape of the failure: points sit mostly above the 45° line under every model. The share of positive alphas ranges from 71% to 88% across the four models, and the mean alpha is positive in each market. A missing risk factor would push some stocks up and others down. A common upward shift is what survivorship produces: the sample is today’s large caps, which are large partly because their returns beat what their risk exposures predicted.
The Sharpe-ratio columns need care. The “tangency” Sharpe ratio is the best in-sample combination of 51 stocks and the factors. With that many assets it is heavily overfitted, which is exactly why GRS is a formal test rather than a comparison of these two numbers.
Adding factors changes the picture surprisingly little. The multi-factor models raise R², so they track month-to-month movements better. But their alphas are not smaller: the CAPM has the lowest root-mean-square alpha of the four. Size, value, momentum, profitability and investment exposures among these large caps do not line up with the gaps between their realised and CAPM-predicted returns.

The CAPM cross-section. The price of beta is 7.1% a year, against a market premium of 4.5% over the same months. The gap (+2.6% a year, t = 0.60) is not significant. The intercept, the excess return of a zero-beta portfolio, is 2.2% a year (Shanken t = 0.54), also indistinguishable from zero. The GLS cross-sectional regression agrees: an intercept of 1.3% (t = 0.51) and a beta premium of 9.5% (t = 1.88). Put simply, the higher-beta half of the sample earned 11.0% a year in excess of T-bills and the lower-beta half 6.8%.
This overturns the earlier ASX-only result. A 16-stock ASX study, measured against an equal-weighted proxy, found a flat security market line, which pointed to Black’s zero-beta CAPM and the “betting against beta” anomaly. With three markets, USD returns and a proper regional market factor, the evidence is instead consistent with the standard Sharpe–Lintner CAPM: zero intercept, slope near the market premium. The honest caveat is power. With 51 stocks and 15 years, the beta premium is not significantly different from zero either (t = 0.94), so the data cannot reject a flat line strongly.
The multi-factor cross-sections do not line up with the factors’ own returns. Value (HML) earned 5.3% a year as a factor, but its price among these stocks is negative in every specification. Investment (CMA) gets a significantly negative price in the five-factor model (-7.6%, Shanken t = -2.23), against a factor mean of 1.6%. The factors are built from all listed stocks in the region, small caps included, and their premia do not show up across 51 large caps.

title: 03 · Testing pricing models: CAPM vs zero-beta CAPM vs Fama–French
text:
Limitations

Survivorship bias. The test assets are today’s large caps. This biases alphas upward for every model, so the GRS rejections overstate how badly the models price the typical APAC stock. A clean test needs the full historical constituent list, including delistings (a target for Module 02).
Individual stocks as test assets. Single stocks have noisy betas and returns. Portfolios sorted on characteristics (size, value, beta) are the standard test assets and give sharper tests, but need fundamentals data for this region.
Regional factors, local stocks. The French factors cover the whole Asia Pacific ex-Japan region, while each stock also moves with its own market and currency. Market-specific factors (Module 05) would be a fairer comparison.
Sample end. The archived factor files end in December 2025, nine months before the rest of the dataset.

title: 05 · Cross-market comparison: ASX vs HKEX vs SGX
text:
Setup: market returns in USD, regional factors
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(tidyverse); library(knitr); library(sandwich); library(strucchange) })
source("../../R/models_linear.R")
source("../../R/data_factors.R")
source("../../R/plots.R")

data_dir <- "../../data/processed"
fx  <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "fx_monthly.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
mkt <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "market_monthly.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
ff  <- get_french_apac("../../data/raw/french")

mk <- names(market_cols)
w <- mkt |> inner_join(fx, by = c("market", "month")) |> inner_join(ff, by = "month") |>
  mutate(ex = (1 + mkt) * (1 + fx) - 1 - RF) |>
  select(month, market, ex) |> pivot_wider(names_from = market, values_from = ex) |>
  arrange(month) |> inner_join(ff, by = "month")
R <- as.matrix(w[, mk]); T_ <- nrow(R); months <- w$month
nw_lag <- 4

# Cross-equation Wald test H0: C b = 0 on a SUR fit (chi-square form)
wald <- function(fit, C) {
  d <- C %*% fit$coef
  W <- drop(t(d) %*% solve(C %*% fit$vcov %*% t(C)) %*% d)
  c(W = W, df = nrow(C), p = pchisq(W, nrow(C), lower.tail = FALSE))
}
# Restriction matrix: coefficient `term` equal in all three equations
equal_across <- function(fit, term) {
  sel <- function(m) as.numeric(names(fit$coef) == paste0(m, ":", term))
  rbind(sel("ASX") - sel("HKEX"), sel("ASX") - sel("SGX"))
}
Market premia and a joint HAC test of equality
mu <- colMeans(R)
V_mu <- NeweyWest(lm(R ~ 1), lag = nw_lag, prewhite = FALSE)   # 3 x 3 HAC covariance of the means
C_mu <- rbind(c(1, -1, 0), c(1, 0, -1))
d_mu <- C_mu %*% mu
W_mu <- drop(t(d_mu) %*% solve(C_mu %*% V_mu %*% t(C_mu)) %*% d_mu)
p_mu <- pchisq(W_mu, 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
se_mu <- sqrt(diag(V_mu))
cor_R <- cor(R)
SUR systems: CAPM and five-factor, with cross-market restrictions
ys <- list(ASX = R[, "ASX"], HKEX = R[, "HKEX"], SGX = R[, "SGX"])
X1 <- cbind(const = 1, MKT = w$MKT)
X5 <- cbind(const = 1, as.matrix(w[, c("MKT", "SMB", "HML", "RMW", "CMA")]))
sur1 <- sur_fit(ys, list(ASX = X1, HKEX = X1, SGX = X1))
sur5 <- sur_fit(ys, list(ASX = X5, HKEX = X5, SGX = X5))

# Identical regressors: SUR point estimates equal OLS (checked), the gain is the joint covariance
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(sur1$coef[c("ASX:const", "ASX:MKT")]),
                           unname(coef(lm(R[, "ASX"] ~ w$MKT))), tolerance = 1e-10)))

resid_cor1 <- cov2cor(sur1$Sigma)
t_beta1 <- equal_across(sur1, "MKT"); t_alpha1 <- equal_across(sur1, "const")
w_beta1 <- wald(sur1, t_beta1); w_alpha1 <- wald(sur1, t_alpha1)
alpha_t1 <- sur1$coef[paste0(mk, ":const")] / sqrt(diag(sur1$vcov))[paste0(mk, ":const")]
stopifnot(all(abs(alpha_t1) < 1.96))   # text: alphas individually insignificant

f5 <- c("MKT", "SMB", "HML", "RMW", "CMA")
eq5 <- map_dfr(f5, \(f) { x <- wald(sur5, equal_across(sur5, f)); tibble(term = f, W = x["W"], p = x["p"]) })
load5 <- tibble(name = names(sur5$coef), est = sur5$coef, se = sqrt(diag(sur5$vcov))) |>
  separate(name, c("market", "term"), sep = ":") |>
  mutate(market = factor(market, levels = mk))
get5 <- function(m, f) load5$est[load5$market == m & load5$term == f]
t5 <- function(m, f) with(load5[load5$market == m & load5$term == f, ], est / se)
Structural breaks: sup-F test and Bai–Perron dating of each market’s regional beta
brk <- map(mk, function(m) {
  df <- data.frame(y = R[, m], x = w$MKT)
  fs <- Fstats(y ~ x, data = df, from = 0.15)
  st <- sctest(fs, type = "supF")
  bp <- breakpoints(y ~ x, data = df, h = 0.15)

title: 05 · Cross-market comparison: ASX vs HKEX vs SGX
text:
Question
Modules 01–04 pooled the three markets. This module compares them directly. Do the ASX, HKEX and SGX earn the same risk premium? Are they exposed to the same factors in the same amounts? Have those relationships been stable? All returns are in US dollars in excess of the US T-bill rate, so that the markets are on a common footing and comparable with the Fama–French Asia Pacific ex Japan factors (as in Modules 03 and 04). Each market is represented by its total-return index ETF (STW, 2800.HK, ES3.SI).

title: 05 · Cross-market comparison: ASX vs HKEX vs SGX
text:
Method
Equal premia. The three mean excess returns are tested jointly, \(H_0: \mu_{\text{ASX}} = \mu_{\text{HK}} = \mu_{\text{SG}}\), with a Wald statistic using a Newey–West covariance (4 lags) that allows for the markets’ strong contemporaneous correlation and for autocorrelation.
SUR. Each market’s excess return is regressed on the regional factors, and the three equations are estimated as one seemingly unrelated regression system,
\[
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf y_{\text{ASX}}\\ \mathbf y_{\text{HK}}\\ \mathbf y_{\text{SG}}\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf X & & \\ & \mathbf X & \\ & & \mathbf X\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol\beta_{\text{ASX}}\\ \boldsymbol\beta_{\text{HK}}\\ \boldsymbol\beta_{\text{SG}}\end{bmatrix} + \boldsymbol\varepsilon,
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \boldsymbol\Sigma \otimes \mathbf I_T .
\]
Because every equation has the same regressors, the SUR point estimates equal OLS equation by equation (a standard result, checked in the code). What SUR adds is the joint covariance of all coefficients, including the correlation of errors across markets. That makes cross-market restrictions testable as one general linear hypothesis, \(\mathbf C\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf 0\). For example, “the same market beta everywhere” is
\[
\mathbf C = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 & -1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix},
\]
which is equivalent to an ANCOVA with market dummies and market × factor interactions. The SUR estimator is hand-written (sur_fit()) and tested against systemfit.
Structural breaks. Rather than imposing dates such as COVID (2020) or the China tech crackdown (2021), each market’s regression on the regional factor is searched for breaks. The Andrews sup-F test asks whether any break exists (trimming 15% at each end), and the Bai–Perron procedure dates the breaks, choosing their number by BIC (strucchange).

Alphas are equal across markets (p = 0.85), and each is indistinguishable from zero (|t| ≤ 0.84). The regional market factor prices all three indices equally well.
Market betas differ (p = 0.00018): 1.08 for the ASX, 0.91 for Hong Kong and 0.86 for Singapore. Part of this is mechanical. The regional factor is cap-weighted over Australia, Hong Kong, Singapore and New Zealand, so it is partly built from the ASX and HKEX. The smallest market, Singapore, has the lowest beta.
Value and profitability loadings differ most. The ASX loads +0.45 on profitability (t = 5.2) and -0.29 on value (t = -3.8). Hong Kong loads -0.69 on profitability (t = -4.4). Singapore loads +0.51 on value (t = 6.2). Size and investment loadings are small and similar across markets.

Comparing 36-month windows ending before Jun 2021 with windows lying entirely after it, Hong Kong’s correlation with the ASX fell from 0.67 to 0.37 and with Singapore from 0.82 to 0.63, while ASX–SGX moved from 0.72 to 0.80. Hong Kong drifted away from the other two.
Only Singapore shows a statistically significant break (sup-F p = 0.00015). The break is dated to June 2021, and Singapore’s beta on the regional market falls from 0.94 to 0.64 after it. Its timing coincides with the start of the Chinese tech and property sell-off from mid-2021, which weighed on Hong Kong and therefore on the regional factor. Because the regional factor contains Hong Kong, a Hong Kong-specific shock can show up as a change in Singapore’s beta. That reading fits the correlations above but is not formally tested here. The ASX and Hong Kong relationships show no significant break, even though individual stocks within them shifted (Module 01): the index-level betas are more stable than their constituents.

title: 05 · Cross-market comparison: ASX vs HKEX vs SGX
text:
Limitations

The regional factor contains the markets. French’s Asia Pacific ex Japan market is a cap-weighted portfolio of these same markets (plus New Zealand). This makes market betas partly mechanical and induces some negative residual correlation. A world or US market factor would avoid this, at the cost of measuring something different.
USD returns include currency. The ASX and SGX results mix equity and currency moves (AUD and SGD against the USD). Hong Kong’s are nearly pure equity because of the peg. Module 01 gives the local-currency view.
Index ETFs. Each market is one ETF tracking a cap-weighted index. The results describe those indices, which are concentrated (banks and miners in Australia, financials and Tencent in Hong Kong, banks in Singapore).
Short sample for premia. Equal premia “not rejected” reflects low power. Distinguishing a 1.5-point difference in annual premia would need many decades of data.
